name: AI in Education
blurb: Artificial intelligence is already in schools, in the tools teachers plan with, the software students practise on, and the systems that run buses and budgets. These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

children.name: Getting Oriented
children.blurb: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: The Classroom
children.blurb: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Every Student, Every Family
children.blurb: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Running the School
children.blurb: Part IV, Running the School, covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members.

sections.body: This part of school life is the whole of a school's use of AI, not just its operations, because a school is also responsible for what AI does to how children learn and for protecting children while it happens. The book describes AI appearing in classrooms, in planning and feedback, in messages to families, and in the business office, from preschool through graduation. It gathers 300 practical ideas across 20 chapters, each carrying an evidence label, and it is honest that the field is young. The evidence it points to shows the same kind of tool producing opposite results depending on how adults designed and supervised its use.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, the book finds, is teachers designing and supervising the tool, tools that give hints rather than answers, a person checking every AI draft, and a person reaching out on every flag a system raises. Weekly messages to families about missed work, grades, and absences cut course failures, and plain supportive notices outperformed legal language, while personal reminders from a student's own counselor helped students reach college. What does not work is leaving students alone with plain chatbots, treating a detection score as proof, and assuming online monitoring prevents harm, and the book says research on young children and students with disabilities is thin. The rule it holds to is that people make every decision that affects a student, that student names and details stay out of any tool without a signed data privacy agreement, and that tools do not change schools, the people in them do.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from orientation to the places where the choices actually get made. Getting Oriented sets up the argument and the rules, so a leader or board member would start there to see how the evidence labels and the five rules run through everything. The Classroom is where a teacher goes for planning, teaching, feedback, and grading, and it is where the Turkey and Nigeria lesson about design and supervision matters most. Every Student, Every Family speaks to parents and to the staff who reach out to them, covering the messages and personal contact that carried the results, and it is where a parent would find what a good school answers. Running the School is for principals and district leaders, covering policy, pilots, purchasing, and professional learning, and it closes the loop by tying the classroom and family work back to the decisions leaders make and the rules they publish.
